evidence.title: A current perspective on daptomycin for the clinical microbiologist.
evidence.abstract: Daptomycin is a lipopeptide antimicrobial with in vitro bactericidal activity against Gram-positive bacteria that was first approved for clinical use in 2004 in the United States. Since this time, significant data have emerged regarding the use of daptomycin for the treatment of serious infections, such as bacteremia and endocarditis, caused by Gram-positive pathogens. However, there are also increasing reports of daptomycin nonsusceptibility, in Staphylococcus aureus and, in particular, Enterococcus faecium and Enterococcus faecalis. Such nonsusceptibility is largely in the context of prolonged treatment courses and infections with high bacterial burdens, but it may occur in the absence of prior daptomycin exposure. Nonsusceptibility in both S. aureus and Enterococcus is mediated by adaptations to cell wall homeostasis and membrane phospholipid metabolism. This review summarizes the data on daptomycin, including daptomycin's unique mode of action and spectrum of activity and mechanisms for nonsusceptibility in key pathogens, including S. aureus, E. faecium, and E. faecalis. The challenges faced by the clinical laboratory in obtaining accurate susceptibility results and reporting daptomycin MICs are also discussed.

evidence.title: Biomimetic Nanomembranes: An Overview.
evidence.abstract: Nanomembranes are the principal building block of basically all living organisms, and without them life as we know it would not be possible. Yet in spite of their ubiquity, for a long time their artificial counterparts have mostly been overlooked in mainstream microsystem and nanosystem technologies, being a niche topic at best, instead of holding their rightful position as one of the basic structures in such systems. Synthetic biomimetic nanomembranes are essential in a vast number of seemingly disparate fields, including separation science and technology, sensing technology, environmental protection, renewable energy, process industry, life sciences and biomedicine. In this study, we review the possibilities for the synthesis of inorganic, organic and hybrid nanomembranes mimicking and in some way surpassing living structures, consider their main properties of interest, give a short overview of possible pathways for their enhancement through multifunctionalization, and summarize some of their numerous applications reported to date, with a focus on recent findings. It is our aim to stress the role of functionalized synthetic biomimetic nanomembranes within the context of modern nanoscience and nanotechnologies. We hope to highlight the importance of the topic, as well as to stress its great applicability potentials in many facets of human life.

evidence.title: Cerebral Mucormycosis without Rhino-Orbital Involvement in a Patient with Chronic Kidney Disease
evidence.abstract: Isolated cases of cerebral mucormycosis demand high clinical suspicion and prompt diagnosis and treatment. In the present case, the patient was a young diagnosed case of chronic kidney disease (CKD) for two years on maintenance hemodialysis, presented with symptoms of headache and increased intracranial pressure, which necessitated both emergency surgical and medical management and was both diagnosed and managed efficiently. Early recognition of clinical and radiological cues with early institution of a medico-surgical approach, with proper containment of underlying predisposing conditions, is vital for managing mucormycosis. The case elucidates that mucormycosis can present as an isolated cerebral abscess without rhino-orbital involvement. CKD should be considered as a possible immunocompromised state predisposing to mucormycosis.

evidence.title: Methods of Complex Resuscitation Measures and Intensive Therapy for Liver Dysfunction - Acute Liver Failure
evidence.abstract:
Abstract

Acute liver failure (ALF) is a rare, life-threatening syndrome characterized by rapid loss of hepatic function in a patient without preexisting cirrhosis, usually with development of coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy. Management requires immediate critical-care resuscitation, organ-support strategies, disease-specific therapies, early recognition of complications (cerebral edema, sepsis, coagulopathy, renal failure), and timely consideration for liver transplantation. This article reviews the definitions and types of ALF, pathogenesis, drugs of choice and their mechanisms, and detailed intensive care resuscitation and management strategies used in contemporary practice. (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov)

 

Definition and types

Definition. Acute liver failure is defined as the rapid development (usually within days to 26 weeks) of severe hepatic injury with impaired synthetic function (INR ≥1.5) and any degree of hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without chronic liver disease. (bspghan.org.uk)

Types / common etiologies.

• Acetaminophen (paracetamol) toxicity — the commonest identifiable cause in many regions.

• Viral hepatitis (A, B, E; less commonly other viruses).

• Drug-induced liver injury (antibiotics, antituberculars, herbal supplements).

• Autoimmune hepatitis.

• Wilson disease, Budd–Chiari syndrome, ischemic hepatitis (shock liver).

• Indeterminate/cryptogenic.

Etiology influences prognosis and specific therapy (e.g., NAC for acetaminophen; chelation/urgent transplant for Wilson disease). (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov)

 

Pathogenesis (brief)

ALF results from massive or sub-massive hepatocellular necrosis and/or apoptosis leading to loss of synthetic (coagulation factors, albumin), metabolic (ammonia clearance, drug metabolism), detoxification, and immunologic functions. Downstream consequences include hyperammonemia and cerebral edema, systemic inflammatory response with vasodilatation/hypotension, renal failure (hepatorenal physiology and acute tubular injury), coagulopathy, and high susceptibility to infections. Cellular mechanisms vary by cause (e.g., oxidative metabolite formation and glutathione depletion in acetaminophen toxicity; immune-mediated injury in autoimmune hepatitis; copper-induced oxidative injury in Wilson disease). The characterization of time‐dependent brittle rock deformation is fundamental to understanding the

time‐dependent deformation through stress corrosion cracking that allows rocks to deform at stresses

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Round 62 capability collision failure; applies to ALL novelty claims)
warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Daptomycin is a lipopeptide antimicrobial with in vitro bactericidal activity against Gram-positive bacteria that was first approved for clinical use in 2004 in the United States. Since this time, significant data have emerged regarding the use of daptomycin for the treatment of serious infections, such as bacteremia and endocarditis, caused by Gram-positive pathogens. However, there are also increasing reports of daptomycin nonsusceptibility, in Staphylococcus aureus and, in particular, Enterococcus faecium and Enterococcus faecalis. Such nonsusceptibility is largely in the context of prolonged treatment courses and infections with high bacterial burdens, but it may occur in the absence of prior daptomycin exposure. Nonsusceptibility in both S. aureus and Enterococcus is mediated by adaptations to cell wall homeostasis and membrane phospholipid metabolism. This review summarizes the data on daptomycin, including daptomycin's unique mode of action and spectrum of activity and mechanisms for nonsusceptibility in key pathogens, including S. aureus, E. faecium, and E. faecalis. The challenges faced by the clinical laboratory in obtaining accurate susceptibility results and reporting daptomycin MICs are also discussed.

Yet in spite of their ubiquity, for a long time their artificial counterparts have mostly been overlooked in mainstream microsystem and nanosystem technologies, being a niche topic at best, instead of holding their rightful position as one of the basic structures in such systems. Synthetic biomimetic nanomembranes are essential in a vast number of seemingly disparate fields, including separation science and technology, sensing technology, environmental protection, renewable energy, process industry, life sciences and biomedicine. In this study, we review the possibilities for the synthesis of inorganic, organic and hybrid nanomembranes mimicking and in some way surpassing living structures, consider their main properties of interest, give a short overview of possible pathways for their enhancement through multifunctionalization, and summarize some of their numerous applications reported to date, with a focus on recent findings. It is our aim to stress the role of functionalized synthetic biomimetic nanomembranes within the context of modern nanoscience and nanotechnologies. We hope to highlight the importance of the topic, as well as to stress its great applicability potentials in many facets of human life.

Abstract

Acute liver failure (ALF) is a rare, life-threatening syndrome characterized by rapid loss of hepatic function in a patient without preexisting cirrhosis, usually with development of coagulopathy and hepatic encephalopathy. Management requires immediate critical-care resuscitation, organ-support strategies, disease-specific therapies, early recognition of complications (cerebral edema, sepsis, coagulopathy, renal failure), and timely consideration for liver transplantation. This article reviews the definitions and types of ALF, pathogenesis, drugs of choice and their mechanisms, and detailed intensive care resuscitation and management strategies used in contemporary practice. (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov)

 

Definition and types

Definition. Acute liver failure is defined as the rapid development (usually within days to 26 weeks) of severe hepatic injury with impaired synthetic function (INR ≥1.5) and any degree of hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without chronic liver disease. (bspghan.org.uk)

Types / common etiologies.

• Acetaminophen (paracetamol) toxicity — the commonest identifiable cause in many regions.

• Viral hepatitis (A, B, E; less commonly other viruses).

• Drug-induced liver injury (antibiotics, antituberculars, herbal supplements).

• Autoimmune hepatitis.

• Wilson disease, Budd–Chiari syndrome, ischemic hepatitis (shock liver).

• Indeterminate/cryptogenic.

Etiology influences prognosis and specific therapy (e.g., NAC for acetaminophen; chelation/urgent transplant for Wilson disease). (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov)

 

Pathogenesis (brief)

ALF results from massive or sub-massive hepatocellular necrosis and/or apoptosis leading to loss of synthetic (coagulation factors, albumin), metabolic (ammonia clearance, drug metabolism), detoxification, and immunologic functions. Downstream consequences include hyperammonemia and cerebral edema, systemic inflammatory response with vasodilatation/hypotension, renal failure (hepatorenal physiology and acute tubular injury), coagulopathy, and high susceptibility to infections. Cellular mechanisms vary by cause (e.g., oxidative metabolite formation and glutathione depletion in acetaminophen toxicity; immune-mediated injury in autoimmune hepatitis; copper-induced oxidative injury in Wilson disease).
